beats.trigger: From Personal to Team
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: You can't really share an agent.
beats.got: Handing over my setup is not the same as handing over something they can use, so I have to choose what to hand over.

beats.trigger: Bring one example from your own organisation where people got access to a tool and did not use it.
beats.got: The module starts from rollouts that failed, which I have plenty of examples of.

beats.trigger: name one person and one test to take out of the room
beats.got: It ends in one person and one test, not a programme. That is better than most.

beats.trigger: And why that one?
beats.got: I am supposed to pick between four things to share. I can't judge them yet.

beats.trigger: Your agent, skill, output or interface is a candidate for hire: does it do the job better than what they currently use?
beats.got: Jobs-to-be-done, which I know from business development. The tool has to beat what the person already does.

beats.trigger: If it could describe anyone in the room, point to the generic line and ask the agent to try that part again.
beats.got: The agent reads my files and writes a job description for a colleague. I check whether it is generic.

beats.trigger: Every picked candidate should name how it moves the teammate's outcome, with infrastructure only as a constraint.
beats.got: Choose by the result the colleague needs, not by what the IT platform supports. That is sensible.

beats.trigger: finds what would stop that candidate from being absorbed and turns it into a technical plan plus a people plan.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Find the obstacle that decides whether the teammate can absorb it, then draft both halves of the plan.
beats.got: Two plans this time, one technical and one for people.

beats.trigger: A good bottleneck explains why several other obstacles stay hard.
beats.got: Find the one obstacle that holds the others in place. This is ordinary root-cause thinking, with an agent doing the sorting.

beats.trigger: A polished technical file beside a people file full of unnamed roles is the finding, not a finished rollout.
beats.got: If the people file has no names in it, the rollout is not ready, however good the technical file looks. I have seen this.

beats.trigger: checks the assumptions underneath these plans, imagines the failure, and writes the first real-world contact
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: The technical and people plans are hypotheses.
beats.got: The plans are guesses until someone tests them. At least it says so.

beats.trigger: what would have to be true for this teammate, doing this job, to fire their current hire and use my candidate?
beats.got: Ask what would make them drop what they use today. It is a useful question.

beats.trigger: Six months from now, the teammate went back to the incumbent.
beats.got: A pre-mortem. The agent writes the failure stories and the strongest one decides what I test first.

beats.trigger: A candidate picked because it fits the infrastructure is shopping.
beats.got: Start from what the person needs and test the switch before building. The line about shopping is fair.

beats.trigger: Lecture: Access is not absorption
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Access is a switch somebody flips, and it completes in a minute.
beats.got: A licence rollout counts as done on day one, but whether anyone uses the tool takes weeks. I have sat through that reporting.

beats.trigger: The proposal got neither a yes nor a no.
beats.got: The author admits an agent project of his own died in a decision meeting. That is more honest than any success story so far, and it is the steering group I know.

beats.trigger: Accountability is the part with a name on it, and a name does not travel inside a folder.
beats.got: Context, boundary and checks can be copied, but the person who answers for the agent cannot. A bit neat, but I agree.

beats.trigger: Pick the one your teammate's week can take in.
beats.got: Each way of sharing needs something different from the receiver. Choose by what their week allows.

beats.trigger: Your candidate is not competing with nothing. It is competing with that.
beats.got: Whatever I want people to use is up against the spreadsheet or the colleague they already have. Every transformation deck forgets this.

beats.trigger: Have the conversation before you build anything more.
beats.got: Talk to one person before building anything else. I can do that.

beats.trigger: Who gets your context, who gets a skill, who wants only the output, and who would use an @mention?
beats.got: Different colleagues need different ways of sharing.

beats.trigger: Access is a switch someone flips. Absorption happens in other people's weeks.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Their answer is the evidence. The plan is still the hypothesis.
beats.got: I bring back what the person said, not the plan. That is a fair ask.

beats.trigger: Next
beats.got: nothing new

take_homes: Access and use are different things. A licence rollout that reports 100% access tells me nothing about whether anyone uses it.
Before pushing a tool at a colleague, find out what they use today and what would make them drop it.
A plan with polished technical files and unnamed people is not ready. I will check my own programmes for that.

monday.move: Pick one team member and ask how they do the job today, and what would make them drop the current way. Build nothing before that conversation.
monday.who: One person from my own team, probably in sales support
monday.when: Probably Tuesday, because Monday is the steering group
monday.stop_condition: If they say the current way works fine and they have no reason to change, I stop and write that down.
monday.blocker: The calendar, and my doubt that this is a different thing from the last three programmes

misconception.why: The module never argues against 'wait and see'. It was honest about how rollouts fail, which I respect, but I saw no demo of anything that was not possible two years ago. The one-conversation test costs me almost nothing, so I might run it. That is a cheap test, not a conversion.

one_line: Less hype than I expected, and the point that access is not use is true, but I still haven't seen what is actually new.
